paragraphs.heading: A change of direction
paragraphs.text: Refraction is the change in a wave's direction as it moves from one material, or medium, into another. Light shows it most often, but sound and water waves refract as well. Prisms and lenses use refraction to steer light, and so does the human eye.

paragraphs.heading: Why light slows down
paragraphs.text: Light travels more slowly in air, glass or water than in a vacuum. The reason is not that it gets scattered or absorbed. As light passes through, it makes charged particles such as electrons wobble, and those electrons send out waves of their own. The original light and these new waves combine into a wave that moves more slowly. Once the light is back in a vacuum, its speed returns to c.

paragraphs.heading: How the bend happens
paragraphs.text: Picture a wave hitting a slower material at a slant. One side of the wave reaches the new material first and slows down before the other side does. With one side lagging, the whole wave swings round toward that side, so it bends away from the surface and toward what is called the normal. Going into a faster material, it swings the other way.

paragraphs.heading: When nothing bends
paragraphs.text: How much a wave bends depends on how much its speed changes and on the angle at which it meets the boundary. A wave that hits the boundary head-on, with its wavefronts lying flat along it, keeps going straight even though its speed changes. Inside a new medium whose properties stay the same, light again travels in a straight line.

paragraphs.heading: Splitting white light
paragraphs.text: A material's refractive index changes with the wavelength of the light. So each color bends by a different angle, an effect called dispersion. When white light passes from air into such a material, its colors fan out. This is how a glass prism, or raindrops in a rainbow, split white light into its spectrum of colors.

paragraphs.heading: The bent pencil
paragraphs.text: Water has a refractive index of 1.33, while air's is about 1, so light bends as it crosses a water surface. Stand a pencil at a slant so it is partly under water, and it looks broken at the surface. The pencil is fine; what bends is the light coming from the water into the air on its way to your eye.
